entry.title: Inside Bevy: How the ECS Scheduler Runs Your Systems in Parallel

link.title: Inside Bevy: How the ECS Scheduler Runs Your Systems in Parallel

entry.content:
Every engine built around a god-object eventually hits the same wall. A GameObject grows a transform, a mesh, a collider, a health value, a script slot, and suddenly every subsystem walks a pointer-chasing object graph, and “can this object move during this phase?” becomes a tribal-knowledge question. Bevy — the data-oriented game engine written in Rust — refuses that design. State lives in flat tables, behavior lives in plain functions, and the compiler enforces who may read or write what. If you have read our tour of Godot, this is the opposite philosophy: no scene tree as the center of the world, just entities and component sets.

So what actually happens on one frame tick? A runner wakes up, a handful of labeled schedules execute in order, each schedule fans its systems out across worker threads, then the render side extracts what it needs and submits GPU commands. Every step is ordinary Rust code you can read in the repository, and the interesting parts are all struct-level decisions: how storage is laid out, how queries cache their results, and where the scheduler inserts synchronization points.

The third question is the boldest: how can thousands of systems mutate the same world concurrently without locks? Bevy’s answer is that it never needs a global lock, because each system declares its data access up front. The scheduler computes disjoint borrows from those declarations and only runs systems in parallel when their accesses provably do not conflict — much friendlier to multicore than, say, a GC runtime where everything shares one heap, like the GIL situation we covered for CPython.

Bevy at a glance: the App drives labeled schedules over a World; archetypal storage feeds cached queries; the executor runs systems in parallel; a render sub-app and the asset server run beside the main loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The whole engine is one builder object. App, L85 owns the main World and the plugin registry; when you call App::run, L185 the App hands itself to a runner function, which for windowed apps is the winit event loop and never returns.
  • A frame is not one function call but a sequence of labeled schedules. Update, L173 sits between PreUpdate and PostUpdate, with Startup and First/Last bookending the loop — all defined in one readable file.
  • The World struct, L96 is the only place state lives. Spawning takes a Bundle, L1243 — a tuple of components — and returns a handle.
  • Storage is archetypal: Archetypes, L777 keeps exactly one archetype per unique component combination, so entities with the same shape sit in contiguous memory.
  • Each archetype points into columnar Tables, L203; components that churn get parked in SparseSets, L780 instead.
  • Queries do not scan the World each frame. QueryState, L85 caches the matched archetype list once and reuses it, which is why iteration cost stays proportional to live matches.
  • The Schedule struct, L413 turns your .before()/.after() hints into an ordering graph, then Schedule::run, L596 executes it — on native platforms via the MultiThreadedExecutor, L86.
  • Rendering is a sub-app, not a phase inside the main loop: RenderApp, L381 gets its own World, and the RenderGraph schedule, L48 chains Begin → Render → Submit → Finish inside it.
  • Assets stream in without blocking: AssetServer::load, L364 returns a typed handle immediately and fills the Assets<T> resource when bytes arrive.

The detail view: how spawning moves entities between archetypes, how the executor splits world borrows, and how the render sub-app and asset server plug into the same World primitives.

One Frame in Bevy: Runner, Sub-Apps, and Schedules

Bevy’s entry point looks deceptively small: App::new().add_plugins(DefaultPlugins).run(). The magic is that a plugin is just data plus a build function — the Plugin trait, L57 requires exactly one build(&mut App) method — so “adding a plugin” means “run its registrations against the App now”, not registering a factory for later.

App::run does something unusual: it mem::replaces the App with an empty one and passes the real App to the stored runner closure. The default runner is the ScheduleRunnerPlugin, L50, a headless loop; winit swaps it for a platform event loop. Either way, each tick calls App::update, L158, which simply calls update() on every SubApp, L66 — the main app first, then the render app.

Why sub-apps? Because the main world and the render world must never fight over the same borrow. App::add_systems, L321 targets the main app’s schedules, while render systems live in the RenderApp’s separate schedule set, each side holding a World that is structurally independent.

Archetypes and Queries: Storage as Columns

Spawning a Bundle does not allocate a heap object. The World finds (or creates) the archetype for that exact component combination, appends each component to its table column, and records the entity’s row location. Adding or removing a component moves the entity to a different archetype — a copy of a few dozen bytes plus an index fix-up, not a rebuild. Hot component data therefore streams through memory like a database scan, which is precisely what makes the ECS fast; this is the data-oriented design that only a language with explicit ownership, like Rust, can hand you without a garbage collector pausing mid-frame.

Archetypes and tables are deliberately decoupled: multiple archetypes can share one table when they differ only in sparse-set components. One quirk worth knowing: archetypes are never cleaned up. The module docs in archetype.rs, L14 note that empty archetypes persist until the World is dropped — so code that rapidly creates unique component combinations accumulates empty shells rather than freeing them. The World even exposes a convenience method that builds and caches a query in one call at World::query, L1862.

The query side is where most engines waste cycles. Bevy’s Query, L488 parameter is paired with a cached state object, initialized once via QueryState::new, L249. That state remembers which archetypes and tables match, so per-frame iteration (QueryState::iter, L1223) walks precomputed lists instead of re-filtering every entity. When a new archetype appears mid-run, the state picks it up and revalidates — an incremental update, not a full rebuild.

The Parallel Scheduler, Sync Points, and Change Ticks

When a schedule builds, each system’s declared Query parameters produce an access fingerprint. Systems whose accesses overlap get ordered relative to each other; systems with disjoint accesses become candidates for parallel execution. At run time the default_executor, L48 picks the multi-threaded path on native platforms, and the executor spawns one task per ready system — you can see the task-per-system pattern at spawn_system_task, L638. No mutex guards the World; instead, systems receive an UnsafeWorldCell whose disjoint-borrow contract the scheduler has already proven.

Two subtleties keep this honest. First, structural changes (spawn, despawn, component add) are deferred: a system queues Commands and applies them later, and Bevy auto-inserts sync points for this — the auto_insert_apply_deferred setting, L1913 controls it, and apply_deferred, L722 is the flush. A sync point is a barrier: systems after it can observe the new state, systems before it ran in parallel underneath.

Second, change detection is just counters. Every component carries Tick, L23 stamps for when it was added and last changed, and the DetectChanges trait, L11 exposes is_changed(). Filters like Changed<T>, L1092 compare those stamps, so “run only when input changed” costs one integer comparison per entity.

The Render Sub-App and Streaming Assets

Rendering runs on its own clock. The RenderPlugin, L161 creates the render sub-app, initializes GPU resources in a RenderStartup schedule, and every frame the extraction step — now factored into its own crate, bevy_extract, L16 — copies just what this frame needs from the main world into the render world. The GPU work itself rides on wgpu, L27, so Vulkan, Metal, and DirectX share one code path; the same backend powers GPU-terminal projects like Alacritty.

Assets follow the same “don’t block” logic. AssetServer::load hands back a Handle, L115 immediately; loaders run through a pluggable IO layer (filesystem, embedded, memory, web), and the Assets<A>, L288 resource resolves handles to loaded data. Any type implementing the Asset trait, L456 gets the whole machinery for free. Because entities hold handles rather than asset data, a texture can still be loading while gameplay code runs — systems simply observe an empty slot until the load completes.

From Cargo Build to First Frame

The repo is a Cargo workspace whose members are declared as crates/* — the ECS, the renderer, and every subsystem are independent crates you can read in isolation. To try it: clone the repo, git checkout latest (a moving tag pointing at the newest release), then cargo run --example breakout — the full arcade game lives at examples/showcase/breakout.rs. For something minimal, examples/3d/3d_scene.rs draws a lit 3D scene in roughly sixty lines. The README’s “hello window” is exactly four statements: App::new().add_plugins(DefaultPlugins).run().

Two build knobs matter in practice. The dynamic_linking feature (declared in crates/bevy_internal/Cargo.toml) turns each crate into a dylib so incremental rebuilds skip relinking the engine; and the multi_threaded feature is what selects the parallel executor — on Wasm the build falls back to the single-threaded one, per default_executor. The full feature matrix is documented in docs/cargo_features.md in the repo root. A plain cargo run --example breakout on a modern desktop takes a few minutes the first time (wgpu and its backends are heavy), then seconds per example afterward.

Honest Limits

Bevy’s README states plainly that it is in the early stages of development, with important features missing, sparse documentation, and breaking changes roughly every three months via the “train” release schedule. The main branch we toured is development code: a large part of the renderer was being reorganized around the render-graph-as-schedule design described in renderer/mod.rs, and extraction was recently pulled into the separate bevy_extract crate — expect churn if you follow along on main.

The engine is also honest about platform gaps: without the multi_threaded feature, or on Wasm, the executor degrades to single-threaded, and App::run never returns on iOS and Web because the platform event loop owns the thread. There is no stable plugin marketplace story and no built-in editor; you compose crates by hand. Development questions route to GitHub Discussions and the Contributor’s Guide in the repo root rather than a formal RFC board, which tells you how young the project still is. None of that blocks studying the code — it just means the architecture you read today may look different next release, and the migration guides at bevy.org are the companion reading this tour assumes.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Bevy's ECS: archetypal storage, cached queries, the parallel schedule executor, the render sub-app, and streaming assets.

entry.title: Inside Godot: How the Scene Tree, Servers, and GDScript VM Actually Work

link.title: Inside Godot: How the Scene Tree, Servers, and GDScript VM Actually Work

entry.content:
You write a small func _process(delta) in GDScript, press play, and a character moves across the screen at a smooth sixty frames per second. It feels like magic, but the whole thing is a precisely choreographed C++ routine that runs inside main/main.cpp on every tick: it splits elapsed wall-clock time into fixed physics steps and one fractional render step, walks your scene tree, drains a queue of rendering commands, swaps GPU buffers, and only then sleeps until the next frame. This post walks that exact path through the engine’s master branch (version 4.8.0, status beta, per version.py), because the best way to stop treating an engine as a black box is to read the loop that never stops running.

The first thing that confuses newcomers is the word “server” everywhere in the tree: RenderingServer, PhysicsServer3D, AudioServer, XRServer, even an AccessibilityServer under servers/display/. For an engine with no networking in sight, that naming looks wrong — until you see what it buys. Nodes never hold GPU handles or solver state. They push opaque resource IDs (RIDs) plus commands into a queue owned by the server, and the server decides when, and on which thread, that work actually executes. It is a client-server split drawn inside one process, which is why the engine can move rendering off the main thread with a boolean instead of a rewrite.

The second surprise is GDScript itself. There is no compile button and no separate build step for your scripts, yet scripts do not run as interpreted text trees either. When a .gd file loads, it is tokenized, parsed into an AST, type-checked, and lowered to a compact bytecode that a register-less Variant-stack VM executes — an interpreter loop in the same spirit as the C eval loop behind /cpython/, except it lives inside the game process and talks directly to engine singletons. Understanding those three mechanisms — the frame loop, the server layer, and the VM — explains almost every “why is it built this way” question you will have about Godot.

Overview of a Godot frame: boot hands control to Main::iteration, which drives the scene tree and the server layer; GDScript bytecode runs inside node callbacks, and physics backends plug in behind an abstract server.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot happens in two phases: Main::setup, L986 parses arguments and registers types, then Main::start, L4056 creates the main loop and loads your project’s main scene.
  • Every frame is one call to Main::iteration, L4967 — physics ticks first, one process pass, then sync and draw.
  • MainTimerSync, L4984 decides how many fixed physics steps this frame owes and what fraction of a step the render pass gets.
  • The scene side is a single SceneTree object whose physics_process, L640 and process, L689 methods fan work out to nodes through process groups.
  • PhysicsServer3D, L391 is a pure abstract interface — step, sync, flush_queries — with the default implementation living in a module.
  • The default solver, GodotPhysicsServer3D::step, L1693, is registered as a plugin; a Jolt backend sits beside it.
  • On the render side, RenderingServerDefault::_draw, L76 is the only place where the frame actually becomes pixels.
  • Script behavior enters the loop at GDScriptFunction::call, L465, the bytecode interpreter that every _process override ultimately runs on.

The same frame in detail: how SceneTree groups and dispatches notifications, how the rendering command queue is drained and executed, and how a GDScript file becomes bytecode before it ever runs.

The Frame: What Happens in One Main::iteration

Main::iteration is the heartbeat, and its ordering is deliberate. After MainTimerSync::advance, L4984 converts elapsed microseconds into an integer count of physics steps plus a fractional process_step, a loop at L5016 runs once per physics tick: it flushes buffered input, syncs the physics servers and flushes their queries (L5036), calls into the main loop’s physics_process (L5047), and finally steps both 2D and 3D solvers (L5081). Physics runs zero, one, or several times per frame — whatever keeps simulation time aligned with real time — while _process runs exactly once.

Then comes the visible half. A single main_loop->process() call at L5108 walks the idle pass, after which RenderingServer::sync() at L5123 drains queued commands and draw() at L5139 produces the frame. Housekeeping follows: GDExtensions tick at L5154, each registered script language gets its per-frame hook at L5158, and AudioServer::update, L1359 mixes the audio graph at L5162. Only at the very end does OS::add_frame_delay, L5228 sleep or spin to hit the target frame rate. If you have ever wondered why a slow _physics_process cascades worse than a slow _process, this order is the answer: physics debt accumulates in fixed chunks, capped by max_physics_steps_per_frame right before the loop.

The Scene Tree Dispatches Notifications, Not Magic

SceneTree is just the MainLoop implementation the engine installs by default, and it does not call your methods directly. It owns ProcessGroup structures; SceneTree::_process, L1260 reorders dirty groups, and SceneTree::_process_group, L1193 does the real work: it sorts nodes by their configured priority, takes a defensive copy of the node list (L1217) so nodes can add or remove themselves mid-iteration, then walks the copy sending notifications — NOTIFICATION_PHYSICS_PROCESS at L1239 or NOTIFICATION_PROCESS at L1246. Nodes that pause or leave the tree are skipped via a can_process() check, which is how the pause menu freezes your game for free.

At the node end, everything funnels through one switch. Node::_notification, L68 maps NOTIFICATION_PROCESS to a virtual script call at L100 — and if your script does not override _process, nothing was ever registered for it, so the cost is a sorted array scan, not a function call. Scene entry works the same way: Node::_propagate_ready, L323 walks children depth-first and only then fires NOTIFICATION_READY at L336, which is why parents are always ready before children fire. Groups are also the engine’s unit of threading: a node can set its process group to sub-thread, and _process_groups_thread, L1254 runs whole groups on worker threads while the main thread handles the rest.

Why Godot Calls Its Backends “Servers”

The server layer is the engine’s firewall between scene code and hardware state. When a Sprite2D changes position, it does not render anything; it updates an RID the renderer already knows about. Those updates accumulate in a command queue, and RenderingServerDefault::sync, L439 is the drain point. When threading is on, init, L276 spawns a pump task on the worker pool whose loop at L419 keeps flushing the queue, and draw, L447 merely pushes _draw onto that same queue — the main thread never touches the GPU API. The draw implementation then runs a fixed sequence: begin the rasterizer frame, update scene and canvas state (L96), draw viewports (L109), end the frame (L115).

The same pattern repeats for physics, and here the abstraction is load-bearing. PhysicsServer3D, L391 declares three pure-virtual methods every backend must implement, and a small manager picks the implementation from project settings at boot. The default solver ships as a module, and the Jolt integration registers itself as an alternative at register_types, L60 — swapping physics engines is a settings change, not a code change. This thin-scene-over-fat-backends design is the same instinct behind the Rust ecosystem’s /rust/ approach of keeping engine systems behind data-oriented boundaries; Godot just expresses the boundary as singletons and RIDs instead of traits.

GDScript: A Bytecode VM Living in the Engine

Loading a script runs a miniature compiler inside the engine. GDScript::reload, L737 drives the whole flow: it feeds the source to GDScriptParser::parse, L448, where a hand-written tokenizer at L482 streams tokens into a recursive-descent parser. The AST then goes through an analyzer that resolves types and flags invalid expressions, and finally through GDScriptCompiler::compile, L3283, which walks each class (L3016) and every expression (L255) while a byte-code generator emits opcodes into a GDScriptFunction. This is why typing a script in the editor feels instant — parsing and analysis run incrementally for diagnostics long before you press play.

Execution is a Variant-stack interpreter with a distinctive trick. GDScriptFunction::call, L465 allocates the stack, then dispatches each instruction through DISPATCH_OPCODE — on GCC and Clang this is a computed goto *switch_table_ops[...] at L394, the same threaded-code technique that keeps interpreter loops fast; MSVC falls back to a plain switch at L409. Everything on the stack is a Variant, engine values are called directly rather than boxed, and a thread-local depth counter at L477 turns infinite recursion into an error. Awaited functions serialize their stack into a state object and resume from a saved instruction pointer, so await works without OS threads. If you have read the interpreter loops behind /php-src/ or browsed how /node/ embeds V8 as a script host, the shape is familiar — Godot just fused the host and the guest into one binary.

From SCons Build to First Scene

Godot builds with SCons, and the entry point is a plain Python SConstruct at the repo root. The two options that matter most are declared there: platform (also -p, auto-detected from your host, at L161) and target, whose choices are editor, template_release, and template_debug with editor as the default (L164). So a local build is:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/godotengine/godot.git
cd godot
scons platform=linux target=editor

The README defers platform specifics to the official compiling docs (README.md, L44), and scu_builders.py reveals a build optimization worth knowing: “single compilation unit” batches translate units per module to cut link times. Every feature module — GDScript, Jolt, Mono, WebRTC — plugs in through its own SCsub and register_types.cpp. Once the binary runs, Main::setup registers server types (L757) then scene types (L789), Main::start parses project.godot, instantiates your main scene under the tree root, and the ready propagation from the previous section fires — first scene alive.

Honest Limits

  • Master is 4.8.0 with status = "beta" in version.py; symbols and line numbers in this post will drift as development continues.
  • GDScript has no JIT: it is an opcode interpreter over Variants, with a computed-goto fast path on GCC/Clang only. The intended escape hatch for hot loops is moving them into C++ behind a server API — the engine’s own code does exactly that.
  • Two full 3D physics backends ship in-tree (godot_physics_3d, jolt_physics), selected by project settings through the manager; their behavior is not identical, and results differ between them.
  • The server split adds a one-frame latency shape: scene changes are queued, and only sync/draw make them visible, which matters when mixing direct server calls with node APIs.
  • The engine carries 59 module directories and a servers/ tree spanning 12 subsystems (audio, camera, debugger, display, movie_writer, navigation, physics, rendering, text, xr) — the source tour here covers the spine, not the skin.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Godot's master branch: how Main::iteration drives a frame, how the scene tree dispatches _process, why backends are called servers, and how GDScript compiles to bytecode.

entry.title: Inside Phaser: The Scene Lifecycle and Step Loop Behind 2D Web Games

link.title: Inside Phaser: The Scene Lifecycle and Step Loop Behind 2D Web Games

entry.content:
A Phaser game ships as one JavaScript bundle and then runs on a five-year-old Android phone, a school Chromebook, and a desktop browser at 144 Hz. That is a strange engineering target for a game engine: no install step, no runtime download, and a memory budget smaller than a single Unity texture atlas. Most engine projects solve this by being small at the core, and Phaser’s answer is visible immediately in its dependency list — the entire runtime depends on exactly one package, an event emitter. Everything else you think of as “the engine” is plain code in one tree that you can read in an afternoon.

So what actually happens in one tick? A browser callback fires, Phaser computes a clamped delta value, runs your scene’s update, steps every physics body, sorts the display list by depth, walks each camera, and flushes the GPU or 2D-context commands — then throws it all away and does it again next frame. The order is not incidental. It is a fixed sequence of events written into a single ~50-line method, and once you see it, every Phaser bug you have met (“my physics are one frame behind”, “my sprite flickers behind the UI”) becomes readable in terms of which stage of the tick ran first.

The other organizing idea is the Scene. If you come from a native engine like Godot, a Phaser Scene is closest to a tree node plus its own update loop, but Phaser generalizes it: every screen, menu, and overlay is a Scene with the same lifecycle — init, preload, create, update — and the engine itself is just a scheduler that steps scenes in one order and renders them in another. This post walks that whole loop through the actual source of the phaserjs/phaser repository, from boot to first pixel.

Overview of the Phaser architecture as built by Game.boot: the TimeStep loop drives Game.step, which fans out to the SceneManager, the renderers, and the manager plugins that hang off each scene's Systems bundle.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot is event-gated. Game.boot, L350 creates the renderer, the DOM container, and the canvas, but the game loop does not start here — it waits for the Texture Manager to emit READY, then calls start.
  • The renderer is chosen once, at boot. CreateRenderer, L44 resolves the default renderType with Features.webGL ? CONST.WEBGL : CONST.CANVAS and throws if the explicitly requested context cannot be created.
  • TimeStep.step, L718 is where the browser hands control over: it clamps negative deltas (a Chrome quirk), optionally smooths the delta to kill frame-time spikes, and only then calls the Game callback.
  • Game.step, L454 is the frame contract: PRE_STEP, user STEP, scene update, POST_STEP, renderer preRender, scene render, postRender — always in that order, every frame.
  • Scenes update in reverse list order and render in forward list order. SceneManager.update, L558 walks the array backwards so an overlay launched later steps after (and can freeze) the scene beneath it.
  • A scene is a status machine, not just a class: bootScene, L473 calls init, resets the loader, runs preload, and only flips the status to RUNNING after create finishes.
  • Rendering is not incremental. Systems.render, L374 depth-sorts the display list and hands it to the cameras on every single frame.
  • Physics and input are not special-cased in the loop — they are scene plugins that subscribe to the same events. ArcadePhysics.start, L130 wires the World to the scene’s UPDATE and POST_UPDATE events and nothing more.

The detail view follows one tick through the call graph: from the TimeStep tick, through Game.step, into the scene status machine, the display list sort, both renderer implementations, the arcade World step, and the input dispatch path.

One Tick: PreStep, Update, Render

The loop begins in Game.start, which binds Game.step into the TimeStep’s animation-frame runner. Each browser tick, TimeStep.step, L718 computes Math.max(0, time - lastTime) — the clamp matters because browsers occasionally report negative deltas — and passes the result through a smoothing step before invoking the callback. This is the only place Phaser cares about real wall-clock time; everything downstream works in the smoothed delta it is handed.

Game.step then emits its event sequence. The interesting decision is what lives where. Global managers like Input and Sound update on PRE_STEP, before any scene logic, so a pointer position is fresh for the frame. Your own game.events handlers get STEP, and only after that does the SceneManager receive update(time, delta). Rendering is deliberately outside the update phase: renderer.preRender clears buffers and applies background colors, then scene.render walks scenes, then postRender handles snapshots. If you have ever written a postrender handler and wondered why the canvas is already “final”, this order is why.

Scenes: Boot, Preload, Create, Update

A Scene instance itself is nearly empty — its constructor just builds a Systems bundle and stores it as this.sys. Everything you actually use in a scene class (add, load, cameras, input, physics, tweens) is a plugin injected into that bundle at init time. That is why the API surface feels huge while the Scene class stays tiny: the class is a namespace, the plugin registry is the engine.

The lifecycle lives in the SceneManager. bootScene, L473 calls scene.init if it exists, resets the loader, and branches: if the scene defines preload, the loader is started and the scene waits; otherwise it jumps straight to create. On loader completion, create runs, the scene’s own update method is bound as the step hook, and the status finally becomes RUNNING — the gate checked by the update loop. Queued scenes are drained by processQueue at the top of every frame, which is how scene.start and scene.launch stay safe to call from inside a running scene.

The update/render asymmetry is the detail most Phaser developers eventually meet. Updates run in reverse list order so that scenes launched later step first — an overlay UI updates before the paused world under it. Rendering runs in forward order so that base scenes paint first and overlays composite on top. Nothing enforces this beyond the two loop directions; it is a pure index-ordering trick that substitutes for a layer system.

Game Objects, Depth Sort, and Two Renderers

Every visible thing is a Game Object registered in the scene’s DisplayList, a typed wrapper over an array. There is no scene graph to traverse by default: draw order is literally list order, and the depth value you set on a sprite is a sort key, not a tree position. Each frame, Systems.render, L374 calls displayList.depthSort() before any drawing happens, so changing a depth mid-update takes effect the same frame — but the sort is a full pass over the list, which is one reason deep scenes get expensive.

Position data follows the same “compute on demand” philosophy. A sprite’s transform component stores x, y, rotation, and scale, and Transform, L494 composes those into a matrix via applyITRS only when something asks for it. Nested containers multiply that through a parent matrix, which is how transforms accumulate without per-object matrix caching.

The two renderers implement the same contract — preRender, render per camera, postRender — from boot time. The WebGL side batches sprite draws into GPU calls and routes each camera’s visible children through render nodes; if you have read how three.js organizes its scene graph for GPU submission, the camera-to-renderer handoff will look familiar, just with 2D batching instead of mesh trees. The Canvas fallback is an immediate-mode 2D-context implementation of the identical interface, which is what lets the same game code run on devices without WebGL support.

From npm Install to First Scene

The repository is a plain Node-style package, and Node tooling is all it needs. package.json declares exactly one runtime dependency (eventemitter3) and builds with webpack: npm run build runs webpack --config config/webpack.config.js, a separate dist script produces the minified release bundle, and npm test runs vitest. The published main entry points at src/phaser.js while the browser field points at the webpack-built dist/phaser.js, so consuming the source directly and the bundle behave differently by design.

TypeScript support is generated rather than hand-maintained: the tsgen script runs jsdoc over the source tree and emits types/phaser.d.ts, then compiles a test project against those types. Unlike reading a compiler that is written in its own language, such as the TypeScript source, the JSDoc comments here are not optional flavor — the same comments are the shipped API documentation and the type surface.

Your first scene, from the engine’s perspective: the config’s scene array is passed to the SceneManager constructor, which immediately queues the class; the first update drains the queue, boots the scene, runs its init and preload, waits for the loader, calls create, and marks it RUNNING. From then on your update(time, delta) is called once per tick until the scene is stopped or sleeps.

Physics and Input: Just Scene Events

The clearest architectural statement in the codebase is that physics does not appear anywhere in Game.step. Instead, ArcadePhysics.start, L130 subscribes the World to the scene’s UPDATE event, and the World maintains its own fixed-step accumulator: it integrates velocity into position only when accumulated elapsed time crosses the frame budget, which keeps simulation speed independent of render rate. The step itself (World.step, L1019) updates every enabled body, reloads the collision tree, and runs the active collider pairs — in that order, so collisions resolve against freshly integrated positions.

The Body-object dance explains the classic “one frame behind” feeling. Each frame, the UpdateList calls preUpdate on registered sprites, and Body.preUpdate, L1127 first syncs the body to wherever its GameObject was placed, then integrates. After collision resolution, the body writes positions back to the GameObjects during POST_UPDATE. Reading input positions happens even earlier, in the PRE_STEP phase handled by the global InputManager, which captures DOM events once and forwards them to per-scene InputPlugins for hit testing.

Honest Limits

The tree is Phaser 4 — package.json reports version 4.2.1 (release “Giedi”) — and Phaser 4’s structure is visible in the source: renderer-side effects live under src/filters and operate on WebGL texture wrappers, so the Canvas fallback path cannot run them; that split is inherent to the two-renderer design, not a missing feature. The CanvasRenderer also describes itself with batching methods that end in immediate 2D-context calls, so performance parity with WebGL is not the goal.

Two more limits worth naming. First, the “engine” is a plugin registry assembled at scene init, which makes the API surface discoverable only through the generated type definitions and JSDoc — the source comments are the documentation, and there is no separate spec to check them against. Second, the fixed-step physics accumulator applies to the arcade World; other scene plugins are driven purely by the frame delta, so mixing subsystems means mixing time models. None of this is hidden — it is all readable in the four files this post linked to — but it is the kind of thing you only learn by reading the source, which is exactly the point of walking it.
entry.summary: How the Phaser source runs a 2D web game: the TimeStep loop, SceneManager lifecycle, depth sorting, arcade physics integration, and the WebGL and Canvas renderers.

entry.title: Inside raylib: How the Minimal C Game Library Draws a Frame

link.title: Inside raylib: How the Minimal C Game Library Draws a Frame

entry.content:
Every newcomer hits the same wall with a full engine: to draw one red circle you inherit a scene tree, an asset importer, an editor layout, and a build system you did not choose. Engines like Godot earn that complexity for large teams, but for a first window, a first sprite, or a lecture demo, the price of admission is simply too high. raylib’s answer is almost aggressive: a handful of C files, one public header, no editor, no scene graph — you can genuinely read the whole thing in a weekend. The obvious question is how a library that fits in your head still talks to a GPU driver, a window manager, and an audio device at the same time.

The two lines every raylib program shares are BeginDrawing() and EndDrawing(). They look like decorative sugar, something you could skip. They are not. Everything between them is recorded into CPU-side buffers, and the second call is where the GPU actually gets fed, where the swap happens, where the frame rate is enforced, and where input events are polled for the next frame. Understanding those two functions is understanding how raylib thinks.

And then there is the portability trick. The same rcore.c that opens a GLFW window on Windows also drives Android, a bare Linux framebuffer via DRM/KMS, and a browser canvas under Emscripten. One file, no #ifdef spaghetti in your application code, because the platform-specific half was split into ten small files behind a fixed contract. This post walks that whole path — from your call to DrawCircleV() down to the raw glDrawElements — using only the actual sources on master.

raylib's module layering: rcore owns the window and the frame bracket, per-platform files own the OS, rlgl owns OpenGL, and the four drawing modules plus raudio sit on top as thin, optional layers.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything the application sees is one header. The version is pinned at RAYLIB_VERSION, L92 — reading “6.5-dev” in a stable-looking library is your hint that master moves fast.
  • rcore is the only mandatory module; optional ones are compiled in or out through switches like SUPPORT_MODULE_RSHAPES, L39 in config.h, which is why the binary can shrink to what you use.
  • The startup chain is short and readable: InitWindow, L591 calls InitPlatform, then rlglInit, then loads the default font — three pages of C, not a framework bootstrap.
  • There is no class hierarchy; all shared state is one global struct, CoreData CORE, L405, which backends and modules both read and write.
  • Window and event code does not live in rcore.c at all: it lives in per-platform files like PollInputEvents, L1311, so the core calls a contract instead of an OS.
  • rlgl defaults to OpenGL 3.3 when no graphics API is defined — see GRAPHICS_API_OPENGL_33, L158 — with explicit escape hatches for GL 1.1, 2.1, ES2 and ES3.
  • Shapes and text deliberately share one texture atlas: SetShapesTexture, L93 hands shapes the font’s white rectangle, so rectangles, circles and glyphs can ride a single batch.
  • Text is not a special path: DrawTextCodepoint, L1302 ends up in DrawTexturePro, exactly like a sprite does.
  • Audio is fully decoupled from the GL side — raudio.c is built on the bundled miniaudio.h, L177 include and would keep playing even if rendering died.

The detail view: follow InitWindow down into InitPlatform and rlglInit, then trace one frame from BeginDrawing through rlVertex3f's CPU buffers to the flush inside EndDrawing.

The Layer Cake: Five Modules and a Header

raylib’s source tree is organized the way its log messages describe it. When InitWindow, L617 starts up it prints the module list — rcore and rlgl marked mandatory, rshapes, rtextures, rtext, rmodels and raudio marked optional. That is not marketing; each module is one compilation unit (or one header) and each can be switched off in config.h before building. The layering is strictly downward: rshapes pushes vertices, rtextures uploads and samples textures, rtext calls rtextures, rmodels drives shaders, and all of them land on rlgl, which alone talks to raw OpenGL. Nothing above rcore knows that a GPU exists.

Inside rcore.c the sections are literal — comments divide Window and Graphics Device (from L544), Screen Drawing (from L857), and Timing (from L1574). If you have ever wanted to know “where would frame pacing live,” the file layout answers before grep does.

rcore: A Frame Is a Timestamp, a Matrix, and a Swap

Look at what the bracket actually does. BeginDrawing, L868 stamps the current time to measure your update phase, resets the modelview matrix with rlLoadIdentity, and applies the screen-scale matrix — that is all. It is cheap on purpose so you can call it once per frame without guilt. Even ClearBackground, L861 is just two rlgl calls to set the clear color and flush the framebuffer bits.

EndDrawing, L885 is where everything deferred gets paid for, in order: first rlDrawRenderBatchActive, L887 uploads and draws whatever vertices your game queued; then SwapScreenBuffer flips the back buffer; then a small timing block computes draw time against the target frame time and calls WaitTime to sleep off the remainder — the frame-pacing system at L896 is the reason a naive raylib loop holds 60 FPS without any of your code. Finally PollInputEvents runs so keyboard and mouse state are fresh for the next frame’s update, and if you pressed F12 a screenshot is written. Camera transitions fit the same pattern: BeginMode2D, L930 must flush the batch before swapping the modelview matrix, because the queued vertices were recorded with the old transform.

rlgl: Immediate Mode, Emulated

The deepest trick in raylib is that rlgl looks like old-school immediate mode but behaves like a modern batched renderer. The whole engine is a header — version stamped RLGL_VERSION, L113 — holding one static state struct, rlglData RLGL, L1118. Startup, rlglInit, L2258, creates the boring-but-critical assets: a 1x1 white texture for untextured shapes, the default shader pair, the default render batch, and a matrix stack explicitly built to emulate OpenGL 1.1.

When rshapes “draws” a rectangle it opens a primitive with rlBegin, L1452 and calls rlVertex2f per corner — but nothing reaches the driver yet. Each vertex is CPU-transformed by the current modelview and appended to plain C arrays inside the batch: rlVertex3f, L1495 writes position, texcoord, normal and color into a preallocated buffer. When that buffer fills, an overflow check hands control to rlCheckRenderBatchLimit, L3205, which drains the batch and quietly starts a new one. rlDrawRenderBatchActive, L3196 is the flush used both by EndDrawing and by any mid-frame texture change, which is how rlSetTexture, L1638 keeps one draw call per texture run instead of per sprite. If you have read how Alacritty batches its glyph grid, this is the same idea — amortize the driver with big vertex streams — arrived at from the opposite direction.

The 3D modules do not ride the quad batch; they bind real programs. DrawMesh, L1491 calls rlEnableShader with the material’s shader id and issues vertex-array draws directly, which is why shaders feel first-class in raylib’s 3D path.

One Contract, Ten Platform Files

The reason rcore.c compiles everywhere is that it never touches a windowing API. InitWindow delegates to InitPlatform, and each file in src/platforms/ implements that contract for one target: GLFW, SDL, RGFW and Win32 for desktop, DRM/KMS for card-slot Linux, Android, two web variants, and even a memory-only framebuffer with no OS. The GLFW backend is the default: InitPlatform runs glfwInit, glfwCreateWindow, L1690 makes the window, and the contract’s swap function is a one-liner — SwapScreenBuffer, L1212 — wrapping glfwSwapBuffers. Time comes from glfwGetTime, L1222, input lands in CORE.Input, and rcore.c neither knows nor cares. The same contract is what lets the web backend feed a browser canvas and the DRM backend drive a framebuffer with no display server at all.

From CMake Build to First Window

The library builds with either toolchain from the src/ directory. With make, the platform is a variable — PLATFORM ?= PLATFORM_DESKTOP, L70 maps to PLATFORM_DESKTOP_GLFW unless you override it with, say, PLATFORM_DESKTOP_SDL or PLATFORM_DRM — and the library type defaults to static via RAYLIB_LIBTYPE ?= STATIC, L89, so make PLATFORM=PLATFORM_DESKTOP RAYLIB_LIBTYPE=SHARED gets you a shared object. With CMake, src/CMakeLists.txt declares the project at PROJECT_VERSION 6.2.0, L3. One honest note for source readers: the Makefile still says 6.2.0 while raylib.h on master reports 6.5-dev — release strings lag the dev branch.

A first window is then deliberately boring: InitWindow(800, 450, "hi"); while (!WindowShouldClose()) { BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); DrawText("frame one", 20, 20, 20, DARKBLUE); EndDrawing(); } — five calls, no callbacks, no objects. The equivalent loop in Bevy gives you an ECS scheduler instead; raylib gives you a while-loop and expects nothing else.

Honest Limits

raylib trades ambition for legibility, and the limits are visible in the tree, not hidden behind documentation. There is no scene graph, no editor, no asset browser, and no animation graph — raylib.h offers types and functions, and the structure of your game is your problem. The rendering backend covers OpenGL variants only (the API switches at rlgl.h, L25 list GL 1.1 through ES3); there is no Vulkan, Metal or DirectX path, so on modern Apple hardware you are living inside MoltenGL-style translation rather than native Metal. The 3D path is honest about its age too: on the GL 1.1 backend DrawMesh, L1452 falls back to client-side state pointers, and 3D meshes are not merged into the 2D-style batch. External dependencies are bundled wholesale in src/external/ — miniaudio, the stb family, glad, cgltf, tinyobj — which is what makes single-file builds possible, at the cost of vendored code that will not update itself. None of this is accidental: config.h, L39 lets you compile the library down to exactly the modules you use. If those trade-offs match your project — a tool, a jam game, a teaching demo, or the rendering core of a Zig side project — the ceiling is low but the floor is remarkably high.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of raylib: how rcore, rlgl, and the platform backends cooperate to turn BeginDrawing/EndDrawing into real OpenGL draw calls.

entry.title: Inside SDL3: How the Cross-Platform Media Layer Absorbs Every OS

link.title: Inside SDL3: How the Cross-Platform Media Layer Absorbs Every OS

entry.content:
Ask anyone who has shipped a native app on three operating systems: the windowing layer is where optimism goes to die. On Windows you fight message loops and DPI, on macOS you fight the main thread and lifecycle events, on Linux you fight Wayland versus X11 before you have drawn a single pixel. Full engines such as Godot carry dedicated platform-abstraction teams just for this layer, and most small studios end up hand-rolling a worse version. Simple DirectMedia Layer has been the shared answer since the 1990s, and the SDL3 rewrite is the most interesting version of it: one small C library that promises window, input, audio, and rendering on two dozen platforms from a single API.

Open the source tree and the first surprise is how the trick works. Your SDL_PollEvent call never talks to the operating system. It reads from a private, mutex-guarded linked list of events that platform threads keep filling up behind your back. Everything OS-specific lives behind compile-time driver tables, so on Linux the video bootstrap contains Wayland and X11 side by side, and your code never learns which one won.

The second surprise is that SDL3 now ships two drawing systems side by side: the classic SDL_Renderer for portable 2D, and the brand-new SDL_GPU API, an explicit, shader-based abstraction over Vulkan, Direct3D 12, and Metal. Understanding when each one loads, and what code runs under each, is the key to reading this codebase. This post walks through both, plus the event queue and the redesigned audio stack, using the actual sources.

SDL3 at a glance: one init path fans out into compile-time platform drivers (video), one global event queue, two drawing stacks (SDL_Renderer over SDL_GPU and friends), and the audio subsystem. Every arrow is a real call direction in the tree.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SDL_internal.h, L63 — every translation unit starts from this one umbrella header, which pulls in the generated build config and the dynamic API shims, so feature flags are decided exactly once per build.
  • SDL_InitSubSystem, L341 — subsystems are refcounted here; asking for video quietly brings up events, keyboard, mouse, touch, and pen.
  • bootstrap, L82 — the video driver table is a plain compile-time array; on Linux both Wayland and X11 sit in it, with Wayland marked preferred next to X11 at Wayland_preferred_bootstrap, L91.
  • SDL_InitVideo, L622 — driver selection honors the SDL_HINT_VIDEO_DRIVER hint first, then walks the table calling each driver’s create function from the loop at L679.
  • SDL_EventQ, L152 — one global queue: a mutex, an atomic count, a live list, and a free list of SDL_EventEntry, L144 nodes that get recycled.
  • SDL_PollEvent, L1602 — literally SDL_WaitEventTimeoutNS with a zero timeout; the waiting logic with joystick pumping and the poll sentinel lives in SDL_WaitEventTimeoutNS, L1732.
  • render_drivers, L109 — SDL_Renderer is itself a driver table: D3D11, D3D12, Metal, OpenGL, GLES2, PS2, PSP, and others, including a modern entry implemented on top of SDL_GPU in src/render/gpu/SDL_render_gpu.c.
  • backends, L319 — SDL_GPU ships exactly three real backends, Metal, D3D12, and Vulkan, chosen at device-creation time.
  • SDL_OpenAudioDeviceStream, L2352 — audio is expressed as streams bound to logical devices; format conversion, buffering, and mixing live in SDL_audiocvt.c, SDL_audioqueue.c, and SDL_mixer.c.

The detail view: platform drivers on the left post into the event queue, init reaches every subsystem, the renderer and GPU stacks select concrete backends, and Linux core glue feeds device hotplug to both video and audio.

One Entry Point, Many Drivers

Every SDL3 program starts the same way: SDL_Init or SDL_InitSubSystem bumps a refcount and initializes what that subsystem depends on. Request SDL_INIT_VIDEO and SDL_InitVideo first spins up events, keyboard, mouse, touch, and pen, then picks a platform driver. The candidate list is the bootstrap array cited above — from Windows, Cocoa, UIKit, Android, and Emscripten to console ports like PS2, PSP, and Vita — and each entry is a tiny struct with a name and a create function pointer. If you pass a driver name via hint, SDL tries each comma-separated candidate; otherwise it walks the table in order and takes the first driver whose create succeeds.

What makes this scale is that SDL never calls the platform again by name. After selection, the library holds a SDL_VideoDevice whose function pointers do everything: pump events, create and destroy windows, manage displays, GL and Vulkan contexts. Window creation shows the modern pattern — the simple SDL_CreateWindow, L2642 just packs its arguments into properties and forwards to SDL_CreateWindowWithProperties, L2416, so one extensible entry point serves every platform without signature churn. The Linux core glue in src/core/linux (udev device scanning, D-Bus for screensaver inhibition) is shared by whatever video and audio drivers got picked, which is why the diagram wires core as its own group rather than part of video.

The Event Queue: How SDL_PollEvent Really Works

The event subsystem is small enough to read in one sitting, and it explains most of SDL’s personality. Platform side, each video driver implements PumpEvents — for Wayland that is the wl_seat dispatch loop in src/video/wayland/SDL_waylandevents.c, for X11 it is the XEvent translation in src/video/x11/SDL_x11events.c. Library side, SDL_PumpEvents, L1595 invokes the driver’s pump through _this->PumpEvents, L1575 and then runs maintenance: updating timestamps, flushing watches.

The queue itself is a doubly-linked list protected by one mutex. Events are pushed either by the driver or by any of your threads via SDL_PushEvent, L1858, which is just SDL_PeepEvents in add mode; the peep function at SDL_PeepEvents, L1270 is the single choke point for add, get, and peek with a type range filter. One clever detail: SDL_WaitEventTimeoutNS pushes a SDL_EVENT_POLL_SENTINEL marker into the queue, so when the drain loop sees the sentinel it knows it caught up and can block on the driver’s wait until the OS wakes something — that is how SDL gives you blocking waits without missing events that arrive mid-drain.

Three consequences for app authors. First, event memory belongs to SDL: the migration guide is explicit that you must copy strings out of drop and text events, since the nodes are recycled. Second, SDL2’s SDL_WINDOWEVENT wrapper is gone — window state changes arrive as top-level events, which the migration notes, L381 describe. Third, watchers registered with SDL_AddEventWatch see events as they are pushed, before any poll.

Two Ways to Draw: SDL_Renderer and SDL_GPU

SDL_Renderer remains the friendly 2D API: create one from a window with SDL_CreateRenderer, L1453, then draw textures and geometry without thinking about shaders. Underneath it is the same driver-table pattern as video — each backend implements texture upload, batching, and present. The backends span old and new: OpenGL and GLES2 for compatibility, D3D11, D3D12, Metal, even PS2 and PSP, plus a pure software rasterizer in src/render/software as the floor. If you know raylib, which solves the same “immediate 2D on a window” problem, SDL_Renderer is the part of SDL that plays that role — including the option to back it entirely by SDL_GPU through the driver in src/render/gpu/SDL_render_gpu.c.

SDL_GPU is the other end of the spectrum: an explicit, render-graph-free API in the Vulkan/D3D12 idiom — command buffers you fill and submit, explicit texture transfer, explicit state objects, swapchains you acquire per frame. The constraint is honest and visible in backends, L319: only Vulkan, D3D12, and Metal are implemented, because those are the APIs worth abstracting in 2026. Selection mirrors video: SDL_GPUSelectBackend, L604 refuses to run unless the video subsystem is already up, honors SDL_HINT_GPU_DRIVER, then asks each backend’s PrepareDriver whether the hardware qualifies before SDL_CreateGPUDevice, L707 instantiates it. Shader inputs are declared per device as SPIR-V, DXBC, DXIL, MSL, or metallib, so you compile offline per target.

A frame looks like: acquire a swapchain texture (SDL_AcquireGPUSwapchainTexture, L3354), record passes into a command buffer, then hand it over with SDL_SubmitGPUCommandBuffer, L3445. Apps like Alacritty that render text with OpenGL cross-platform had to solve this window-plus-GPU plumbing themselves on top of winit; SDL3 packages the same machinery for C.

Audio Without Callbacks: Devices, Streams, Mixers

SDL3’s audio redesign leans on a small number of verbs. Enumerate hardware with SDL_GetAudioPlaybackDevices, L1571 — physical devices, the real outputs your OS knows about. Opening one with SDL_OpenAudioDevice, L2004 yields a logical device; bind one or more SDL_AudioStreams to it, and SDL_OpenAudioDeviceStream, L2352 is the one-call shortcut that does both. The stream is where SDL3’s value lives: it accepts whatever format, sample rate, and channel count your data is in, and the conversion machinery in SDL_audiocvt.c (backed by the ring buffers of SDL_audioqueue.c) reshapes it to the device’s format. For mixing into the final output there is SDL_mixer.c, and for last-word DSP you can attach a callback with SDL_SetAudioPostmixCallback, L2135, which runs over the device thread’s mixed float buffer.

The old callback-centric API is gone on purpose: SDL2’s SDL_LockAudioDevice/SDL_UnlockAudioDevice pair was removed because there is no user callback thread left to protect — streams maintain their own locks and are documented as safe from any thread. That also means SDL3 will not implicitly initialize the audio subsystem when you open a device; you must call SDL_Init(SDL_INIT_AUDIO) yourself. Backend coverage matches the video story: WASAPI on Windows, coreaudio on Apple, and pulseaudio, ALSA, JACK, and PipeWire among the options on Linux, with hotplug events when udev or the OS reports changes.

From CMake Build to First Window

The documented build is three commands. On Windows, per the README, L24: cmake -S . -B build, then cmake --build build --config RelWithDebInfo, then cmake --install build --config RelWithDebInfo --prefix C:/SDL. On UNIX the same flow installs to /usr/local with sudo cmake --install build --prefix /usr/local. Useful switches: -DSDL_TESTS=ON builds the test programs, -DSDL_EXAMPLES=ON the examples, and -DSDL_SHARED/-DSDL_STATIC pick library flavors. The repo even ships a 67-line hello.c demonstrating the callback style.

Then a game links it via find_package(SDL3 REQUIRED CONFIG REQUIRED COMPONENTS SDL3-shared) and target_link_libraries(mygame PRIVATE SDL3::SDL3), or vendors the source with add_subdirectory. In hello.c, SDL_MAIN_USE_CALLBACKS replaces main with SDL_AppInit, SDL_AppEvent, and SDL_AppIterate; init calls SDL_CreateWindowAndRenderer("Hello World", 800, 600, SDL_WINDOW_FULLSCREEN, ...) — note the title moved into the first parameter in SDL3 — and the event callback returns SDL_APP_SUCCESS on SDL_EVENT_QUIT or a keydown, ending the app without you managing a loop at all. For comparison, Rust projects like Bevy consume the same platform services through their own windowing layer; SDL3 keeps that whole layer in one C library you can vendor and forget.

Honest Limits

SDL3 is a breaking rewrite, and the migration guide is the honest map. SDL_RenderCopy became SDL_RenderTexture and returns bool (migration, L1412); SDL_CreateWindow no longer takes a position; fullscreen is now an explicit mode set with SDL_SetWindowFullscreenMode, and SDL_WINDOW_FULLSCREEN_DESKTOP is gone. The SDLmain library was replaced by the header-only SDL_main.h. Event memory is owned by SDL. Each of these will break an SDL2 codebase that compiles cleanly, and the dynamic API does not paper over them.

SDL_GPU’s scope is a genuine limitation, not a bug: three backends means Vulkan-class, D3D12-class, or Metal-class hardware only. There is deliberately no OpenGL implementation, so old GPUs and some emulated environments fall back to SDL_Renderer or software. Backend selection also depends on video being initialized first — calling SDL_GPU before SDL_INIT_VIDEO fails by design. Finally, the CMake FAQ notes that on Linux the build requires X11 or Wayland development packages unless you explicitly opt out, and per-driver feature coverage still varies; the README-wayland and README-linux docs list the caveats per platform. SDL3 absorbs the differences, but reading the per-platform docs before shipping remains part of the job.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of SDL3: the video bootstrap table, the event queue, SDL_GPU vs SDL_Renderer, audio streams, and how platform backends hide every OS behind one C API.

entry.title: Inside SFML: How the Module System Turns Vertices into Pixels

link.title: Inside SFML: How the Module System Turns Vertices into Pixels

entry.content:
If you have ever written a 2D game against raw SDL, you know the ritual: create a window, create a renderer, fill a rect, call SDL_RenderPresent, and only then start worrying about textures, blending, and scaling. SFML hides all of that behind a single line of code — window.draw(sprite) — and somehow it still feels fast. That combination of “one obvious call” and respectable performance is exactly why C++ developers keep picking it up. But when a call is that short, the interesting engineering is invisible, and invisible engineering is what this blog is about.

The answer to “what does draw() actually do” lives in a deliberate piece of C++ architecture: sf::RenderWindow inherits from sf::Window and from sf::RenderTarget at the same time. The Window half owns the operating-system window and the OpenGL context; the RenderTarget half owns the vertex path that feeds that context. Everything you draw goes through one choke point — RenderTarget — and everything about how SFML feels is decided inside that choke point: which GL state gets set, when it is cached, and how many function calls a sprite costs.

We cloned the master branch of SFML/SFML (version 3.x, C++17, built with CMake 3.28 or newer) and traced the full journey of a vertex: from sf::Sprite, through sf::RenderTarget, down to a raw glDrawArrays call. Along the way we found a rendered-out audio backend, a five-way platform split for GL contexts, and a state cache whose design notes are literally written into the source as a comment block. The two diagrams below map the whole system; every claim in this post links to the exact source line that backs it.

Overview of the five SFML modules and the spine that connects them: System feeds Window, Window feeds Graphics, and Audio and Network stand alongside as independent modules.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The System module is deliberately tiny: sf::Time is a header-only constexpr value type with seconds()/milliseconds() factories (Time.hpp, L41), and it is the currency the rest of the library pays its timing in.
  • sf::Window::create() pairs two platform objects: a WindowImpl for OS events and a GlContext for rendering (Window::create, L85). That pairing is the whole Window module in one line.
  • GlContext::create() funnels every platform through a shared-context manager that instantiates a ContextType — WGL, GLX, or EGL — and locks a mutex while doing it (GlContext::create, L576). GL entry points are loaded with glad (GlContext.cpp, L34).
  • sf::RenderWindow is the marriage of the two worlds: its constructor deliberately routes around the base-class constructor (“it contains virtual function calls”) and calls Window::create() directly (RenderWindow::RenderWindow, L40), then onCreate() initializes the render-target half (RenderTarget::initialize, L117).
  • Every drawable object implements one pure virtual method, draw(RenderTarget&, RenderStates) (Drawable.hpp, L66). That interface is the only contract between game code and the renderer.
  • A sprite is not an object on the GPU. It is four CPU-side vertices uploaded as a TriangleStrip, with its texture and transform stuffed into RenderStates (Sprite::draw, L117).
  • The choke point: RenderTarget::draw(const Drawable&) is two lines long — it just calls back into the object (RenderTarget::draw, L342) — while the vertex-array overload next door does the real GL work.
  • The chain ends at drawPrimitives(), which maps SFML’s six primitive types onto OpenGL modes and issues the single glDrawArrays call that puts pixels on screen (RenderTarget::drawPrimitives, L890).
  • Audio has its own spine: sf::SoundBuffer decodes a whole file into PCM and reattaches every live sf::Sound using it when the buffer changes (SoundBuffer::update, L267), and the playback engine underneath is vendored miniaudio, not OpenAL (Miniaudio.cpp, L32).

The overview shows the skeleton, but the skeleton is not where SFML earns its “fast” reputation. For that you need the detail view, where the platform backends, the FBO implementation, and the streaming audio classes all become visible.

The detailed view: per-platform GL contexts (WGL/GLX/EGL), the RenderTarget draw flow with its FBO path, the miniaudio playback stack, and the Network socket family.

Five Modules, One Library

SFML’s source tree under src/SFML contains exactly six directories: System, Window, Graphics, Audio, Network, and a small Main helper for Android entry points. The dependency direction is strictly downward — Graphics calls into Window and System, Audio and Network call into System, and nothing calls up. This is what makes the CMake options in the root CMakeLists.txt honest: SFML_BUILD_WINDOW, SFML_BUILD_GRAPHICS, SFML_BUILD_AUDIO, and SFML_BUILD_NETWORK are independent toggles (CMakeLists.txt, L49), so you can link just sfml-window if you only need input and a context, which is precisely the setup many raylib and raw-GL projects use SFML for.

The split between sf::WindowBase and sf::Window is subtler and easy to miss. WindowBase owns everything that does not need OpenGL: the OS window handle, the event pump, and the pollEvent() loop, which since SFML 3 returns a std::optional<Event> (WindowBase::pollEvent, L142). Only sf::Window adds the GlContext. If you have ever embedded a rendering context into a GUI toolkit or a terminal emulator like Alacritty, you know why this boundary matters: window management and GL context ownership are two different fights, and SFML refuses to conflate them. An engine like Godot solves the same problem with a platform-abstraction layer hundreds of classes wide; SFML solves it with inheritance and two classes.

What draw() Actually Does

Call window.draw(sprite) and this is the exact chain. First, RenderTarget::draw(const Drawable&, const RenderStates&) performs virtual dispatch into the object, which multiplies its own transform into the states and hands back raw vertices (RenderTarget::draw, L342). The Transformable base class keeps position, rotation, scale, and origin as scalars and recombines them into a 3x3 matrix only when somebody asks — and caches the result until a setter dirties it (Transformable::getTransform, L122). So a static sprite costs zero matrix math per frame; a moving one costs one 3x3 multiply.

Then the vertex-array overload of draw() takes over (RenderTarget::draw, L349). If the batch is small enough, SFML pre-transforms the vertices on the CPU into an internal cache and later issues the draw with an identity modelview matrix (RenderTarget::draw, L358) — a neat trade of GPU matrix work for CPU pointer writes. setupDraw() then reconciles the desired state with what the GL state machine already holds: view, blend mode, stencil mode, texture, and shader are each rebound only if they changed since the last call (RenderTarget::setupDraw, L818). A long comment block at the bottom of the file explains each of these caching strategies, including why textures are tracked by a custom ID rather than a raw GL name — because GL IDs can be recycled after deletion (RenderTarget.cpp, L925).

Finally, the fixed-function GL calls land: glVertexPointer, glColorPointer, and optionally glTexCoordPointer describe the interleaved sf::Vertex layout (RenderTarget::draw, L394), and drawPrimitives() translates the primitive type enum and fires glDrawArrays (RenderTarget::drawPrimitives, L890). Every GL call is wrapped in glCheck, which logs errors in release builds and can be made fatal with a CMake flag. sf::RenderTexture reuses this exact machinery with a different backend: an FBO implementation that binds and unbinds framebuffer objects instead of the window surface, sharing all of the state-cache code.

From CMake Build to First Window

Building SFML from this tree is a two-command affair. The project requires CMake 3.28 as its floor (CMakeLists.txt, L1) and compiles as C++17 via target_compile_features(SFML PUBLIC cxx_std_17) (CMakeLists.txt, L281). Configure with -DSFML_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON if you want the sample programs (CMakeLists.txt, L394), or use -DSFML_USE_SYSTEM_DEPS=ON to link system freetype/vorbis/flac instead of the bundled ones (CMakeLists.txt, L112). The README recommends the official CMake project template, which downloads and builds SFML alongside your application (readme.md, L14) — a FetchContent flow that sidesteps manual installation entirely.

Now trace what happens between sf::RenderWindow window({800, 600}, "Title"); and the first frame. The constructor calls Window::create(), which first closes any existing window, then creates the platform WindowImpl (Window::create, L85) and the GlContext with your requested ContextSettings — depth bits, stencil bits, anti-aliasing level, version flags. Inside GlContext::create(), a process-wide shared context is created once and mutex-guarded; the new context is then instantiated as the platform ContextType and initialized against the requested settings (GlContext::create, L576). Back in RenderWindow, onCreate() records which framebuffer binding counts as the window’s default (important when FBOs are available) and runs RenderTarget::initialize(), which sets up default views and generates the unique ID that the state-tracking map uses to know whether this target is already active in the current context (RenderTarget::setActive, L483).

The event loop is the third piece. while (window.pollEvent(event)) pulls platform messages out of the WindowImpl queue through the std::optional-returning API, and window.display() flips the backbuffer by calling into the context (Window::display, L196). If you set a framerate limit, display() also sleeps out the difference between the frame time and the limit using the System module’s clock (Window::setFramerateLimit, L168). That is the entire runtime contract: pump events, draw, display.

Audio Without OpenAL

The most surprising thing in the Audio module is what is not there: OpenAL. Through SFML 2.x the audio stack was famously built on OpenAL, but SFML 3 removed the shared-library requirement entirely (the changelog records “Removed OpenAL shared library requirement” as a 3.0 change (changelog.md, L247)). The replacement is miniaudio, a single-file C library that SFML vendors and compiles directly into itself — the file literally contains #include <miniaudio.c> (Miniaudio.cpp, L32). For a game developer this means one less runtime DLL to ship and no more “OpenAL32.dll not found” support threads.

The data flow is classic resource/handle separation. sf::SoundBuffer owns decoded PCM samples for short sounds: its constructor throws sf::Exception if the file fails to load (SoundBuffer::SoundBuffer, L44), loading goes through sf::InputSoundFile, which dispatches to per-format readers for WAV, OGG/Vorbis, FLAC, and MP3 (SoundBuffer::loadFromFile, L108). The clever part is buffer mutation while playing: update() detaches every sf::Sound currently using the buffer, recomputes the duration, and reattaches them (SoundBuffer::update, L267) — the destructor does the same swap-then-detach dance to avoid iterator invalidation (SoundBuffer::~SoundBuffer, L93). Long audio takes the other path: sf::Music is a sf::SoundStream, which decodes the file in chunks on a background thread and never holds the whole PCM in memory. sf::Sound::play() just forwards the state change down to the miniaudio-backed implementation (Sound::play, L218).

Sockets, Packets, and Blocking Modes

The Network module is the smallest, and its design is the most conservative: thin RAII wrappers over BSD-sockets with a portable SocketSelector on top. sf::TcpSocket::connect() takes an IP address, port, and a sf::Time timeout, and returns a status enum rather than throwing (TcpSocket::connect, L840). Raw sends and receives return the number of bytes actually transferred so partial writes can be handled (TcpSocket::send, L1079). On top of the raw byte layer sits sf::Packet, which adds length-prefixed framing and stream operators so a send(packet) call transmits your typed payload as one message (TcpSocket::sendPacket, L1264). sf::TcpListener::accept() hands out connected sockets, sf::UdpSocket handles datagrams, and the selector multiplexes them all — enough to build a small authoritative server without pulling in a networking dependency.

Honest Limits

Reading the source also makes SFML’s boundaries clear, and the repository is refreshingly upfront about them. First, the rendering path is not a modern core-profile renderer: the code drives compatibility-style GL calls — client-side vertex arrays with glVertexPointer/glColorPointer, glMatrixMode/glLoadMatrixf for the projection — rather than shaders-and-VBOs everywhere (RenderTarget.cpp, L394). It is fast for 2D, but if you want GPU-resident batches the escape hatch is sf::VertexBuffer, and anything fancier means writing your own GL code against the context SFML hands you.

Second, version 3 is a real break with 2.x, and the migration guide spells it out: sf::Event is now a variant polled through std::optional, enumerations are scoped, sf::Angle replaces bare float degrees, and the C++ standard floor moved (migration.md, L169). The README states plainly that development is focused on version 3 in master and that no more features are planned for 2.x (readme.md, L9) — so codegen targets and tutorials aimed at 2.x will fight you. Third, scope: this is a 2D library; there is no scene graph, no 3D math, no asset tooling — the README describes the modules as windowing, graphics, audio, and network, nothing more. And fourth, the license: the code is zlib/libpng, free for commercial use with no attribution required, but the project ships it strictly “as-is, without any express or implied warranty” — the same disclaimer header sits at the top of every source file you just read.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of SFML's five modules - Window, Graphics, System, Audio and Network - and how window.draw() becomes an OpenGL draw call.

entry.title: Inside three.js: From Scene Graph to WebGL Draw Calls

link.title: Inside three.js: From Scene Graph to WebGL Draw Calls

entry.content:
Every three.js developer eventually hits the same three walls. First, a mesh you just added simply does not render — no error, no warning, just an empty canvas. Second, you change a single material flag like needsUpdate and the frame hitches for a hundred milliseconds. Third, renderer.render(scene, camera) looks like one function call, yet something in there manages matrices, lights, shadows, shaders, and hundreds of draw calls.

All three mysteries resolve the same way: by reading the source. The answers live in a handful of files under src/ — and none of them are magic. An invisible mesh is usually the renderer silently dropping your object at one of its four checkpoints (visible, layers, frustum culling, or a program that never got compiled). The hitch after needsUpdate = true is a full GLSL recompile triggered by a cache-key miss. And the one render call is a fixed, readable sequence of stages.

This post walks that flow in the current dev branch — from the scene graph down to gl.drawElements — with every claim pinned to a real file and line.

Overview: the six stages between renderer.render() and a WebGL draw call. Every node is a real file in the src/ tree.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Scene is a thin container. Scene, L40 is just a background field, next to environment at L50 and fog at L59. Rendering semantics come almost entirely from Object3D.
  • Everything in the graph is an Object3D holding a local matrix and a derived matrixWorld; the world matrix is computed as parent.matrixWorld × matrix at L1207. Scene inheritance is bookkeeping, not rendering.
  • render(), L1641 is the orchestrator. It syncs matrices (L1666), walks the graph via projectObject, L1723, sorts the results (L1730), renders shadow maps (L1749), then draws three queues.
  • projectObject, L1873 never draws. It only filters (visible at L1874, layers.test at L1876) and pushes render items into WebGLRenderList, L54 via push, L122.
  • Materials never compile themselves. The renderer asks WebGLPrograms, L54 for a parameter bag, hashes it into a cache key (L411), and only acquireProgram, L642 constructs a new WebGLProgram on a miss.
  • GPU buffers are lazy. projectObject calls objects.update(), L1911, which flows through WebGLObjects, L5 into attribute uploads that only send changed ranges (WebGLAttributes, L80).
  • One GL state machine sits under it all. Before each draw, setProgram resolves uniforms and state.useProgram, L2587 binds the compiled program. WebGL is a state machine, and three.js wraps it in exactly one cache layer.

Detail view: the same flow expanded — matrix contract, traversal, three render queues, the program cache, buffer bookkeeping, and the two draw paths.

One render() Call, Six Stages

Strip away the XR and output-pass branches and render() is a strict sequence. First, matrix sync: scene.updateMatrixWorld() runs if scene.matrixWorldAutoUpdate is true (L1666), then the camera updates its own chain. Second, per-scene render state and render list are fetched and re-initialized (L1704) — these are pooled per scene, not allocated per frame. Third, projectObject fills the list. Fourth, the list sorts. Fifth, the shadow map pass re-uses the collected light array (L1749). Sixth, three queue passes execute: opaque, transmissive, transparent (L2001). The order is the contract: culling runs against final camera matrices, and lights are gathered before any material asks “how many directional lights do I have?” Notably, this entire flow is target-agnostic: whatever setRenderTarget, L2960 last selected receives the draws, which is how shadow maps, transmission passes, and post-processing effects reuse the exact same stages instead of duplicating them.

The Scene Graph Is a Matrix Contract

Object3D.updateMatrixWorld, L1194 is the whole story of why objects appear where they do. If matrixAutoUpdate is on, the local matrix recomposes from position/quaternion/scale. If matrixWorldNeedsUpdate or force is set, matrixWorld is rebuilt from the parent chain (L1207) — and the dirty flag propagates downward by forcing children to recompute. That is why an object whose ancestors moved still lands in the right place: dirtiness flows down the tree in one pass.

Two practical consequences fall out of this code. If you set matrixAutoUpdate = false for performance and forget to call updateMatrix() after moving an object, the renderer will faithfully draw your stale matrix — nothing warns you. And frustum culling tests geometry.boundingSphere, not vertices: Mesh.intersectsFrustum, L236 compares the sphere against the frustum, computing it lazily if null (L258). If you overwrite position attributes at runtime without updating the bounding sphere, the renderer may cull an object that is right in front of the camera — the fourth invisible-mesh checkpoint, and the least obvious one.

Finally, the per-draw matrices are derived, not stored: for each render item, modelViewMatrix is recomputed as camera.matrixWorldInverse × object.matrixWorld (L2172). The scene graph does not know about cameras; the draw loop does.

projectObject: Culling and Bucketing

The traversal function (L1873) is a recursive switch on object type. For every node: bail if not visible (L1874), then a bitwise layers.test against the camera (L1876) — layers are the cheap way to render subsets of a scene without restructuring it. Meshes, lines, and points additionally survive only if ! object.frustumCulled || object.intersectsFrustum( frustum ) (L1926). Lights take a different branch entirely: they are pushed into the render state (L1890), which is why light collection is free of the render list.

Survivors become render items in WebGLRenderList: three plain arrays — opaque, transmissive, transparent (L59). The bucket decision is one branch on material.transparent (L140). Sorting then runs two strategies: painterSortStable, L1 draws opaque front-to-back (early-Z rejects hidden pixels), while reversePainterSortStable, L31 draws transparent back-to-front so blending composes correctly. The third queue exists because refraction needs the opaque frame as input — transmissive objects render in a separate pass. Note the renderer never sorts geometry within a mesh; sorting granularity is one draw item.

How a Material Becomes a GLSL Program

This is the caching story behind your needsUpdate hitch. getParameters, L54 folds the material type (a shaderID lookup at L62), the light counts from render state, fog, environment, morph attributes, and precision into a plain parameter object. getProgramCacheKey, L411 serializes every parameter and boolean into a string — that string is the shader identity.

The renderer’s getProgram, L2210 keeps a Map per material keyed by that string (L2246) and early-outs when the program and the light-state version are unchanged (L2252). On a miss, acquireProgram consults the global programsMap (L644) — two materials with identical state share one program — and only then constructs a WebGLProgram (L652).

Inside WebGLProgram, the GLSL is assembled textually: #include chunks are expanded and loops unrolled (L752), light counts are baked into the source, then gl.linkProgram runs (L820) with driver diagnostics collected when debug.checkShaderErrors is on (L825). So material.needsUpdate = true does not “refresh” anything — it forces a new cache key and a full compile.
