The mitigation is pre-warming: renderer.compile(scene, camera) (L1400) walks the graph once and pays the compile cost before the first visible frame.

The Last Mile: Buffers and Draw Calls

After a program is chosen, each item falls through to renderBufferDirect, L1200. Inside, three things happen in order: setProgram runs (or reuses) the shader for this exact material/camera/scene combination (L1206), state.setMaterial configures blending, depth, and face culling — including flipping the winding order when a mesh has a negative-determinant world matrix — and finally the index buffer decides which draw path fires. If material.wireframe is on, the geometry’s index buffer is transparently swapped for a wireframe attribute that WebGLGeometries synthesizes and caches (L158); the draw range is then doubled to account for the expanded index list.

The buffer layer beneath is deliberately lazy and differential. objects.update(object) (WebGLObjects, L5) refreshes the geometry and any instanced attributes like instanceMatrix (L32); WebGLGeometries.get registers a dispose listener per geometry (L62) so GPU memory is reclaimed the moment a JavaScript geometry is garbage-collected — no manual cleanup API to remember. And uploads are partial: WebGLAttributes.updateBuffer, L80 merges adjacent or overlapping updateRanges before sending only those slices with gl.bufferSubData. Editing 1% of a large position attribute does not re-upload the other 99%. Two draw implementations finish the job — non-indexed geometry goes through drawArrays, indexed through drawElements — and both increment the counters you see in renderer.info.

From npm Install to First Frame

The dev workflow is unusually minimal. npm run dev runs node utils/build/dev.js && node utils/server.js -p 8080 (package.json, L50). The build step writes five re-export stubs into build/ — three.module.js is literally one line re-exporting src/Three.js — so during development there is no bundler at all; the dev server serves the real src/ files, and imports resolve through the ./src/* package export (L17). The optimizing production build is separate: npm run build invokes rollup (L47). The test suite is browser-driven — npm test chains eslint with two Puppeteer-based unit runners (L46). A first frame therefore needs only: create renderer, add meshes, call setAnimationLoop (L1613) with render() inside — and optionally compile() first if startup jank matters. If you enjoy this kind of source dive, the Godot scene tree and Bevy ECS are the two most instructive peers; the Node tooling here and the TypeScript typing ecosystem around three.js are worth a look too.

Honest Limits

The rendering path described here is the WebGLRenderer path, and it has hard edges. WebGL 1 is gone: passing a WebGL 1 context throws “WebGL 1 is not supported since r163” (L102). The WebGPU renderer lives in the same tree (WebGPURenderer, L28) and ships as a separate build artifact via the ./webgpu export (L18), but it does not use the WebGLPrograms cache or the GLSL assembly described above — it is the Node/TSL material system with its own backend. On the CPU side, both painter sorts run every frame when sortObjects is true, so tens of thousands of transparent items are a JavaScript sorting cost, not a GPU one. And culling granularity is exactly one object with one bounding sphere: no occlusion culling, no portal systems — three.js deliberately leaves spatial partitioning to you.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of three.js: how the scene graph is traversed, frustum-culled, sorted, shader-cached, and turned into WebGL draw calls.

entry.title: Inside Alacritty: How a GPU-Accelerated Terminal Emulator Renders Your Shell

link.title: Inside Alacritty: How a GPU-Accelerated Terminal Emulator Renders Your Shell

entry.content:
Open a half-gigabyte log file with cat in a typical terminal and the interface starts to melt: keystrokes echo late, the scrollbar fights back, and a CPU core saturates. Run the same command in Alacritty and it stays smooth. The difference is not shell trickery or clever output buffering — it is an architectural decision made in 2017 and refined since: keep terminal state on the CPU, but let the GPU composite every frame.

“GPU-accelerated terminal” sounds like marketing, so it is worth pinning down what it actually means. A terminal’s job is to turn program bytes into a grid of styled characters, then put that grid on screen. Most of the cost is bookkeeping: parsing escape sequences, maintaining scrollback, and redrawing the visible slice. When that bookkeeping is paired with a renderer that uploads rasterized glyphs once into a GPU texture and afterwards only pushes a few thousand textured quads per frame, the parser and the paint loop stop competing for the same resources. Everything in Alacritty’s design follows from that separation.

Between the moment your shell writes a byte to the pseudoterminal and the moment a pixel lights up, the data crosses five stages: PTY read, escape-sequence parsing, grid mutation, damage collection, and GPU draw. This article walks each stage through Alacritty’s actual source on master — every symbol and line number below links into the upstream repo at the version current when written (binary crate 0.18.0-dev). It is all Rust, using the 2024 edition with a toolchain floor of 1.85.

Alacritty's data flow: the binary crate wires windows and input; a dedicated "PTY reader" thread parses shell bytes into the shared Term; the grid stores cells; the renderer turns damaged cells into GPU draws. Click any node to open the file on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Two crates, one screen. The workspace holds four members members, L2: the GUI binary, the window-free alacritty_terminal library, and two config helper crates. The library gates its tty and event_loop modules off for wasm targets wasm gates, L8, which is why its terminal logic can be tested headlessly against recorded byte streams.
  • The main thread owns windows, not I/O. Startup builds a winit event loop whose user events are Alacritty’s own Event type EventLoop::with_user_event, L138, then one WindowContext per window creates the shell’s PTY tty::new, L201 and spawns the I/O thread event_loop.spawn, L227.
  • Bytes are parsed straight into state. pty_read leases the shared FairMutex, reads chunks from the PTY, and calls parser.advance to mutate Term in place pty_read, L103, parser.advance, L153.
  • One Wakeup per burst. After a parse burst the loop sends a single Event::Wakeup Wakeup, L166 instead of one per write — so a fast prompt like Starship redrawing on every command coalesces into one frame.
  • The grid is a ring buffer. Scrollback rotates by moving an index, not memory Storage, L33.
  • Damage before pixels. Display::draw pulls per-line damage damage(), L458 and merges it into the frame’s DamageTracker before any GL call Display::draw, L775.
  • Two shader backends. GLSL3 versus GLES2 is chosen at startup from the context’s shader version backend selection, L146 — the same “detect the hardware, pick the cheapest correct path” philosophy that tools like ripgrep apply to CPU work.

A closer cut: the I/O loop's read and write paths around the FairMutex, Term's escape-sequence handler callbacks, the ring-buffer Storage, and the renderer's backend selection feeding the glyph atlas.

The Workspace: a Library That Happens to Ship a GUI

The first thing worth understanding is the crate boundary. alacritty_terminal contains the entire terminal state machine — grid, cells, scrollback, selection, vi-mode cursor — with zero knowledge of windows, GPUs, or keyboard events. The alacritty binary crate then adds the platform layers: winit for windows, glutin for the OpenGL context glutin, L31, crossfont for rasterizing fonts, and an input Processor Processor, L77 that maps key and mouse events onto bindings or PTY writes.

That boundary pays off twice. First, the library ships reference tests that replay raw byte recordings into a Term and diff the resulting grid snapshot — dozens of .recording plus grid.json pairs live under alacritty_terminal/tests/ref/, covering VT cases from tab stops to 24-bit color. Second, the state machine cannot drift toward UI concerns: if a feature needs a window, it must live in the binary crate and talk to the library through the event proxy — EventProxy wraps a winit EventLoopProxy and implements the library’s EventListener trait EventProxy, L2072.

Stage One: Shell Bytes Become Terminal State

A pseudoterminal (PTY) is a kernel object: the shell runs on the slave side while the emulator holds the master, reading bytes programs print and writing bytes you type. On Unix the master is an openpty with a child-exit watcher unix Pty, L102; on Windows the same trait set is implemented over ConPTY ConPTY, L110. Both backends expose EventedReadWrite, so either can be polled without busy-waiting.

The I/O thread’s heart is EventLoop::pty_read pty_read, L103. Its speed trick is a lock protocol: the thread first leases the terminal lock lease, L116 and only escalates to a blocking lock when its read buffer is full try_lock, L139. The renderer holds the same FairMutex only for the microseconds it takes to snapshot cells. Under a cat flood, the parser can churn through megabytes while the UI thread still wins the lock regularly — the reason the interface stays responsive.

Parsing itself is delegated to the external vte crate, re-exported from the library root pub use vte, L23. Term implements the Handler trait for every escape family impl Handler, L1059: cursor moves, SGR color changes, scrolling regions, insert and delete lines. The parser never allocates strings it doesn’t need; it just drives those callbacks over the incoming bytes.

Output to the shell flows the other way through a Notifier Notifier, L333, which funnels the terminal-side Event enum Event enum, L14 — PtyWrite, Resize, Shutdown — into the I/O loop’s channel, where pty_write drains it toward the PTY. The terminal pushes UI-relevant events like title changes through its event proxy; grid changes wake the renderer once per burst.

The Grid: Scrollback as a Ring Buffer

Everything the handler mutates lands in a Grid<Cell> Grid, L110: a cursor, a display_offset for how far you’ve scrolled back, and the raw rows. Term actually holds two grids — the primary screen and the alternate screen Term, L268 — because that is how full-screen TUI programs work. When fzf takes over your terminal, it activates the alternate grid Term struct grids, L281; when it exits, the primary grid — and your scrollback — reappears untouched.

The storage behind the grid is the quiet highlight. Naive scrolling memmoves thousands of rows; Alacritty’s Storage<T> Storage, L33 instead keeps rows in a plain Vec<Row<T>> plus a zero field marking which element is currently the bottommost line zero field, L41. Rotation becomes a modular index update — the comments call it out explicitly against slice::rotate_left’s memory rearrangement rotate doc, L17 — and shrinking scrollback only trims the logical length, deferring reallocation. Each row is a fixed-width Row<T> Row, L17.

Each Cell is deliberately tiny: a char, foreground and background colors, and a Flags bitmask Cell, L141 packed as u16 bitflags Flags, L22. Wide characters, zerowidth marks, hyperlinks, and underline colors are rare, so they hide behind an Option<Arc<CellExtra>> — the common cell stays flat, and grids copy cheaply. Scrollback defaults to 10,000 lines scrolling_history, L359, adjustable from config.

Finally, mutation and rendering communicate through damage. Term accumulates a TermDamageState: a “fully damaged” flag plus per-line (left, right) column ranges. damage() damage(), L458 hands those out — always adding both the old and new cursor positions — and reset_damage() reset_damage(), L489 clears the slate. A fast full-screen rewrite marks everything; a single printed character damages one line segment.

Stage Two: Damage-Aware GPU Rendering

Display Display, L342 owns the OpenGL context, the glyph cache, and the DamageTracker DamageTracker, L16. Each draw() begins by snapshotting RenderableContent RenderableContent, L27 — the visible slice of the grid resolved into RenderableCell values with final colors RenderableCell, L189 — then merges the terminal’s damage into the frame tracker, plus UI overlays like search or the visual bell. A telling detail: the Term lock is dropped before any GL work drop lock, L815, so parsing resumes while the frame is being built.

Which shader backend runs is decided once at context creation: GLSL3 when the context offers shader version 3.3 or newer on desktop GL, GLES2 otherwise backend selection, L146, overridable from config. Both implement the same TextRenderer trait TextRenderer, L48; the difference is subpixel antialiasing, which the GLES2 path must split across three shader passes.

Text is drawn as textured quads over one GPU resource: the glyph atlas Atlas, L33. It is a square RGBA texture where glyphs are packed row by row, tracking row_extent, row_baseline, and row_tallest as the allocator state. Atlas::insert Atlas::insert, L119 either fits the glyph or returns Full/GlyphTooLarge AtlasInsertError, L64, and the cache above it rasterizes on demand GlyphCache, L46 — first use of a glyph costs a CPU rasterization; every later frame is just a texture lookup. Cells are batched by atlas texture; a batch flushes when the texture changes or the batch fills batch flush, L119, keeping draw calls low on dense output. Underlines, strikes, and the cursor are layered on afterward as rectangle geometry cursor rects, L896.

From Cargo Build to First Prompt

The fastest path is cargo install alacritty — platform libraries still apply. From a source checkout, the build is cargo build --release cargo build –release, L242, producing target/release/alacritty binary path, L256. The release profile enables thin LTO.

System dependencies are the usual suspects for GUI code in Rust: on Debian/Ubuntu, cmake g++ pkg-config libfontconfig1-dev libxcb-xfixes0-dev libxkbcommon-dev python3 deps, L86; on Windows, the MSVC toolchain plus Clang 3.9 or newer Windows, L229. On Linux/BSD the windowing backends are compile-time features — default ["wayland", "x11"] default features, L88 — and you can force just one with --no-default-features --features=wayland (or x11) feature flags, L250. On macOS, make app produces an app bundle, with make app-universal for an x86+ARM binary.

Two post-build steps complete the setup: installing the terminfo entry with sudo tic -xe alacritty,alacritty-direct extra/alacritty.info terminfo, L298 so programs emit sequences Alacritty understands, and dropping the binary onto your PATH. Launch it and the WindowContext machinery from the first diagram runs: PTY spawned, I/O thread started, the first Wakeup turns into your prompt.

Honest Limits

  • No tabs, no splits — by design. The README FAQ states plainly that you won’t find “tabs or splits (which are best left to a window manager or terminal multiplexer)” nor a GUI config editor tabs FAQ, L104. Multiplexing is delegated to tools like tmux.
  • “GPU-accelerated” is not a benchmark claim. The README itself says throughput is quantified with vtebench while latency and frame consistency are “more difficult to quantify,” and that some terminals intentionally slow down to save resources — test your own workloads vtebench, L86.
  • OpenGL only. Rendering sits on glutin with EGL/WGL and two GL shader backends; there is no wgpu or Vulkan backend in this tree glutin, L31.
  • Version state. The checkout behind this article is 0.18.0-dev, an unreleased development snapshot, so cited line numbers will drift as development continues.
entry.summary: A source-code tour of Alacritty's architecture: the PTY event loop, the grid ring buffer, ANSI parsing, damage tracking, and the OpenGL glyph atlas that draws your shell.

entry.title: Inside fd: How the Fast Rust Find Replacement Walks Your Filesystem

link.title: Inside fd: How the Fast Rust Find Replacement Walks Your Filesystem

entry.content:
Every developer knows the ritual: you want the file named foo, and out comes find . -iname "*foo*" -not -path "*/node_modules/*". Quotes because find’s argument order is a trap, -iname because you do not remember the casing, and a -not -path filter because find happily descends into directories you told git to forget. Then you run fd foo — no quotes, no flags — and the answers scroll by instantly, case-insensitively, already skipping everything your .gitignore covers. The difference is not cosmetic; it is architectural.

What actually happens in the milliseconds between pressing Enter and the first path appearing? Most people imagine a single loop: walk the tree, test each name against the pattern, print. fd’s real answer is a small distributed system: a clap-derived option parser, a smart-case decision, a compiled matcher, a configurable WalkBuilder, a pool of worker threads pushing batches through a bounded channel, and a receiver thread that silently chooses between “sort everything” and “stream now” modes.

This post walks fd’s actual source (v10.5.2, the master branch) to explain how each stage works and why the stages are ordered the way they are. If you have read our ripgrep deep dive, some of the machinery will look familiar — fd borrows the same ignore crate that powers ripgrep’s walker, and the borrowing is explicit in the code.

Overview: fd splits into a CLI layer, a matcher builder, the parallel walk core, shared data types, and the printing stage. One bounded channel connects walkers to the receiver.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup is a single function: run, L83 parses Opts, L39 via clap derive, translates flags into one immutable Config, L14, and ends by calling walk::scan — fd has no long-lived state between these stages.
  • Pattern mode is decided up front by determine_pattern_type, L226: regex by default, --glob, --exact, or --fixed-strings; the same routine also powers smart case at L106, where a pattern containing any uppercase character silently re-enables case sensitivity.
  • build_patterns, L73 compiles your strings once into a RegexSet, a GlobSet, or the trivial MatchAll; for multiple --and patterns a name must satisfy every regex, enforced by the count check at L30.
  • build_walker, L345 is where speed policy lives: hidden files, ignore rules, depth limits, symlink handling and the thread count are wired into ignore’s WalkBuilder, finishing with build_parallel() at L400.
  • spawn_senders, L441 registers one filtering closure per worker thread; results are grouped into pointer-sized BatchSender, L73 batches so the channel moves Arc<Mutex<Vec>> handles rather than one message per entry.
  • Backpressure is a single line: bounded(2 * config.threads), L621. When the receiver falls behind, the channel fills and the walker threads simply block — no unbounded memory growth on huge trees.
  • The receiver is a ReceiverBuffer, L128 that waits on recv_deadline, L186: if 100 ms pass without completion it flips to streaming, and if the walk finished inside the window, stop, L280 sorts the buffer first.
  • Thread count defaults to default_num_threads, L804 — available_parallelism() capped at 64 so fd does not spawn 128 threads on a big build server for a search that finishes in 20 ms.

Detail view: the startup stages on the left feed the walk core; the filter closure in the middle orders checks from cheapest to most expensive before anything is sent across the channel.

From Cargo Build to First Search

fd is a single small crate, which makes the build story unusually legible. The package is named fd-find (Cargo.toml, L16) while the binary it installs is fd (L29) — that split is why the install command is cargo install fd-find even though you type fd afterwards. The crate targets edition 2024 and requires Rust 1.90.0 (L20), so a current stable toolchain (see our Rust tour) is enough: cargo build --release produces the binary directly, or cargo build for a fast debug build that only records line tables for dependencies.

The release profile is tuned for a CLI tool: lto = true, strip = true, codegen-units = 1 (L90) — smaller binary, fewer jumps, no symbol table for a tool whose entire job is to start fast. Feature flags matter too: the default set is ["use-jemalloc", "completions"] (L95), and use-jemalloc swaps in the tikv-jemallocator global allocator, but only behind a long cfg gate in main.rs, L48 that excludes Windows, macOS, Android and a few embedded targets — macOS is disabled on purpose due to a jemalloc bug (Cargo.toml, L66). A base feature exists for packagers who want just the allocator. The heavy lifting comes from the dependency list: ignore = "0.4.28" (L37), crossbeam-channel (L45), regex, globset and memchr — the same BurntSushi crates you would find under the hood of ripgrep, which is no coincidence given the shared flag heritage documented in cli.rs, L109.

The Parallel Walk: One WalkBuilder, N Threads

The heart is ignore::WalkParallel. scan, L602 opens the channel, then spawns the receiver and lets walker.run(...) occupy the remaining threads. There is no manual work distribution: WalkParallel hands each thread directory entries as it discovers them, and every thread runs the same closure built inside spawn_senders, L441. Two atomic flags — quit_flag and interrupt_flag (WorkerState, L304) — let a Ctrl-C handler or an early exit (a --quiet match, a full --max-results quota) tell every worker to return WalkState::Quit on its next entry (L458).

The closure’s first lines are micro-decisions that add up. The depth-0 root entry is skipped (L478) so fd lists contents, not the directory itself. A --ignore-contain check tests for sentinel files before any other work, explicitly to save syscalls (L462). And when the walker hands over an Err for a broken symlink, fd does not give up: broken_symlink_from_err, L643 unwraps the error chain, confirms the target was a symlink via symlink_metadata, and rebuilds it into a printable entry — so broken links still show up in results.

Filtering: Cheap Checks Before Expensive Syscalls

The worker closure is essentially an ordered gauntlet, and the order is the optimization. First patterns.matches_path, L507 tests the file name against the compiled matcher — pure CPU, zero syscalls, so most junk entries are rejected before the OS is ever asked a question. Only then come the filters that need metadata, each gated behind an Option so a search without -e, -t, -S or --changed-within pays nothing for them.

The extension filter checks entry_path.file_name() against a RegexSet of patterns like \.rs$, built once during startup (main.rs, L330, case-insensitive). File-type selection delegates to FileTypes::should_ignore, L50, which implements -t d/f/l/x/e/s. Owner (Unix-only) comes next, then size, where SizeFilter::is_within, L69 compares against +500m/-2g-style bounds parsed with SI and binary prefixes at startup (L35). Time filters run last before output: TimeFilter::applies_to, L57 accepts durations (2h), dates, or @epoch seconds, and all supplied constraints must pass. Crucially, the metadata each of these needs is not fetched repeatedly: DirEntry caches it in a OnceCell (dir_entry.rs, L91), so a size filter followed by a time filter costs one stat, not two. A surviving entry is colored in the worker thread (L578) — even LS_COLORS styling is moved off the single receiver.

.gitignore Rules and –unrestricted

The reason fd “just works” in a repository is that build_walker configures the ignore crate to interpret git’s own ignore machinery: .git_ignore, .git_global, .git_exclude (walk.rs, L355) plus parent-directory rules — the same semantics git uses when deciding what to commit, which our git internals tour covers from git’s side. One subtlety is require_git: by default fd only honors .gitignore files when it is inside an actual git repository (L358), a deliberate choice to avoid surprising ignore behavior in plain folders. fd adds two custom layers git does not have: .fdignore registered via add_custom_ignore_filename (L366) and a global ignore file at ~/.config/fd/ignore (L369).

All of it is switchable. --no-ignore (-I) disables the ignore stack, and -u/--unrestricted (cli.rs, L137) is a single-keystroke alias for --no-ignore --hidden, mirroring ripgrep’s -u. The --exclude globs are implemented separately from ignore files, as a gitignore-style Override built with a ! prefix per pattern (build_overrides, L328) — so excludes compose with, rather than replace, repository rules.

The 100 Milliseconds That Sort Your Results

Printing has a hidden decision you never see. The receiver starts in Buffering mode (ReceiverMode, L26) and accumulates entries up to MAX_BUFFER_LENGTH = 1000 (L123). Each recv call carries a deadline of 100 ms (DEFAULT_MAX_BUFFER_TIME, L125); if the deadline fires first, the mode flips to Streaming and the buffer is dumped unsorted — for a huge tree you get results immediately, sorted-ness be damned. But if the entire walk completes inside the window, stop() sorts the buffer before printing (L282). That is why small searches come out alphabetically ordered and multi-second ones do not: fd bets that most searches finish faster than a human notices, and pays sorting only when it is free.

Everything downstream is also batch- and lock-aware. receive wraps stdout in a BufWriter (L433), flushes opportunistically when the channel runs dry, and print_entry, L17 handles hyperlinks, colors, custom separators and --format templates. For --exec, the receiving side changes shape entirely: with per-result execution fd clones the receiver onto every thread (L414) and the sender drops its batch size to 1 (L447) to spread commands evenly, while batch-mode --exec keeps big batches.

Honest Limits

fd is a filename finder, and it does not pretend otherwise. Nothing in src/ reads file contents — there is no content-search module — so greping inside files is out of scope by design; pair fd with a content tool, which is exactly the division of labor between fd and ripgrep. Consequences follow from that scope: a pattern containing / cannot match a bare file name, so fd raises a friendly error suggesting --full-path instead of silently returning nothing (main.rs, L176).

Default behavior has sharp edges worth knowing. Ignore rules apply only inside git repositories unless you pass --no-require-git (cli.rs, L96); hidden files mean only leading-dot names (cli.rs, L40) — macOS’s resource forks or Windows system attributes are not “hidden” to fd; and smart case is evaluated per-pattern, with fixed/exact strings falling back to a plain uppercase scan (patterns.rs, L118). Platform quirks are documented in the tree: --list-details shells out to ls and errors on Windows without GNU ls installed (main.rs, L453), and the jemalloc allocator is compiled out on macOS and Windows entirely (Cargo.toml, L66). None of these are bugs — they are the cost of the single-crate, do-one-thing design that makes the source above worth reading in an afternoon.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of fd: how the ignore crate's parallel WalkBuilder, a cheap-first filter chain, gitignore handling and a 100 ms output buffer make fd so fast.

entry.title: Inside the fish Shell: How Typed Characters Become Running Jobs

link.title: Inside the fish Shell: How Typed Characters Become Running Jobs

entry.content:
Open fish for the first time, type git che, and a gray ghost of a full command appears at the end of your line — a real suggestion pulled from your history, not a canned prefix. Press the right-arrow key and it lands in your buffer. No plugin manager, no ~/.fishrc incantation, no four-hour rabbit hole. That “it just works” feeling is the surface of a very deep machine, and the machine is worth opening.

The moment you press Enter, that friendly line editor transforms into something closer to a compiler backend: the buffer is tokenized, parsed into a typed tree, expanded through five distinct stages, packaged into a Job of Process structs, assigned a process group, and handed to posix_spawn or fork. A piped command like grep error log/**.log | wc -l is not “run” — it is assembled, piece by piece, from data structures fish has been mutating since before you finished typing.

One more reason this tour is timely: fish was famously a C++ codebase for two decades, but fish 4.0 ported the core to Rust (the changelog tracks it as issue #9512). Today’s master contains no C++ sources at all — just Rust crates, a workspace Cargo.toml declaring version 4.9.3, and the Rust 1.85 MSRV. Reading the source now means reading Rust.

The whole journey at a glance: the interactive reader on the left feeds the parser, expansion turns strings into candidates, and the execution layer turns the AST into real processes — all backed by layered shell state.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup is tiny. The binary entry point main, L349 parses flags, decides whether the session is interactive, and calls reader_read, L549 on stdin. Everything users associate with fish — prompt, suggestions, colors — hangs off that single call.
  • The reader parses while you type, not just after Enter. read_i builds a config with syntax_check_ok: true (read_i, L824), so the buffer is continuously parsed for live highlighting and error marking — the dashed edge from the reader back into the parse tree in the diagram.
  • One parse function serves everything. Interactive evaluation, fish -c, config files, and even the highlighter all funnel through parse_source, L257, which calls ast::parse, L1400 to build a JobList tree and wraps it in a ParsedSource, L109 that keeps the original string alive for source ranges.
  • Expansion is a stage machine, not a regex soup. expand_string, L201 drives separate stages for tilde, variables, braces, command substitution, and wildcards — each stage can multiply the candidate list.
  • A Job is built before anything runs. run_1_job, L1546 creates the job object (Job::new, L1665) and only then calls exec_job, L1695. Construction and execution are cleanly separated.
  • Process groups are a first-class concept. Every job carries a JobGroup, L59 holding the pgid, terminal-ownership flags, and a cancel signal — this is what makes Ctrl-C hit the whole piped command and not fish itself.
  • Universal state sits at the bottom of the stack. EnvStack, L212 layers variable scopes; the EnvUniversal, L41 database feeds the universal layer, which is why set -U survives restarts and crosses fish instances.

The detail view: each group in the overview unpacks into the real modules — the readline event loop, the parse tree, the five expansion stages, the spawn path, and the state stores.

Tokenize, Parse, and the Rust AST

Fish’s grammar is unusual among shells because it is typed rather than ad hoc, and the Rust rewrite doubled down on that. The Tokenizer, L238 first turns raw source into a flat stream of TokenType, L18 values — strings, pipes, redirections, ends — handling quoting and escape rules that date back two decades.

Then the interesting part happens. Instead of an interpreter wandering over tokens, ast::parse, L1400 runs a Populator that directly fills Rust structs: a JobPipeline, L767 is one chain of piped commands, AndorJob, L1007 captures and/or chaining, and a DecoratedStatement, L954 is one command with its sudo-style decorators. The result is a strongly-typed tree rooted at JobList (Ast, L1445) — there is no void * node soup, so the compiler itself rejects malformed tree walks.

The Parser, L390 then does evaluation. Its eval_with, L524 parses the string and hands the tree to eval_node, L630, which constructs an ExecutionContext, L119 and dispatches: job lists to run_job_list, L1795, if/while/for to their dedicated run_* methods. Syntax errors are therefore impossible past this point — the doc comment on eval_parsed_source, L561 says exactly that: “Because the source has been parsed, a syntax error is impossible.”

Expansion: Five Stages Before Anything Runs

A fish argument like ~/$project/*.{rs,toml} is not a string — it is a plan that explodes into dozens of real arguments. The expansion layer implements that plan as an ordered stage machine inside expand.rs: stage_cmdsubst, L1389, stage_variables, L1436, stage_braces, L1476, home-directory expansion at stage_home_and_self, L1480, and finally stage_wildcards, L1497.

The stages are honest about their jobs. expand_tilde, L348 consults the environment for $HOME and ~user. expand_variables, L608 implements fish’s signature list semantics — one variable can expand to many arguments, with slices like $list[1..3]. expand_braces, L845 does the Cartesian product. Command substitution (expand_cmdsubst, L969) is special because it must execute code, so it calls into the execution layer — you can see the edge from expansion to exec_subshell_for_expand in the detail diagram.

Wildcards get their own module because they are the only stage that touches the filesystem. wildcard_expand_string, L1021 walks directory trees to materialize matches for * and the recursive **, while wildcard_match, L1078 does the filtering and wildcard_has, L1165 decides whether a string is a glob at all. If you like this layer, the fast path-friendly sibling tool in this series — ripgrep for searching — solves adjacent problems with the same rigor.

From a Job to a Living Process

Execution begins as bookkeeping. run_1_job, L1546 checks --no-execute, records the executing node for profiling, and applies per-job variable assignments before Job::new, L1665 assembles a Job, L613 — a sequence of Process, L365 structs, each tagged with a ProcessType, L55 of external, builtin, function, or block. Only when the whole job is described does exec_job, L86 start it.

exec_job is where the pipe plumbing lives. Its comment explains that up to three pipes can be “in flight” — the one to read from, the one to write to, and the one for the next process — and the loop over processes wires them up, passing each to exec_process_in_job, L1222. That dispatcher routes to exec_builtin_process, L1187 for builtins and exec_block_or_func_process, L1054 for functions, both of which run inside the fish process, recursively re-entering the parser.

External commands take the spawn path. exec_external_command, L861 builds argv/envv, computes a PgroupPolicy (lead a new group, join the job’s pgid, or inherit fish’s), and prefers posix_spawn via PosixSpawner, L96 because it is faster than fork on systems like macOS; otherwise fork_child_for_process, L692 takes over. Meanwhile the JobGroup, L59 tracks whether the job wants the terminal and who is foreground, so job control — suspending, resuming, Ctrl-C — behaves. Finished jobs are collected by job_reap, L983, and wait waits through proc_wait_any, L1115. The pairing of a shell with a fast terminal emulator — alacritty, for instance — only matters because fish is this careful about who owns the tty.

The Reader: Autosuggestions and Highlighting

The interactive layer is the part you actually see. The event loop is Reader::readline, L2570: it consumes CharEvents, applies key bindings resolved through BindingSet, L298, and repaints the screen. Every edit triggers update_autosuggestion, L5591, which asks the persistent History, L1191 store for a matching prefix and then validates it — autosuggest_validate_from_history, L355 re-runs the suggestion through the highlighter to avoid proposing commands that would fail. Pressing right-arrow calls accept_autosuggestion, L5670. Tab completions flow from complete, L2534 into the Pager, L90, and the coloring itself is produced by highlight_shell, L96, which is why invalid commands turn red before you press Enter. If you enjoy that interactive-selection workflow, fzf composes beautifully with fish’s history pager, and starship plugs into the same prompt-event hook fish exposes.

Universal Variables: State That Follows You

set -U EDITOR vim works across every open fish and every future fish. The keeper of that promise is EnvUniversal, L41, which tracks modified keys in a dirty set and writes them via sync, L162 to a single file resolved by default_vars_path, L627 — the fish_variables file in your config directory. Cross-instance awareness comes from a small family of notifier backends; on Linux the notifyd-based NotifydNotifier, L28 watches that file so a second fish session picks up changes without polling. Exported universal variables additionally bump an export generation count, visible right in the struct’s fields.

From Cargo Build to First Prompt

Building fish from source is a standard Rust workflow wrapped in a thin CMake shell, and the README, L116 states the requirements plainly: Rust 1.85 or later with cargo, CMake 3.15+, a C compiler for feature detection, and a network connection since dependencies download automatically. The canonical install path (README, L140) is:

mkdir build; cd build
cmake ..
cmake --build .
sudo cmake --install .

CMake exists because fish needs system feature detection, but underneath it drives cargo: the workspace root Cargo.toml declares the fish binary at src/bin/fish.rs, alongside fish_indent and fish_key_reader, and pins the workspace to edition 2024. The compiled binary needs no runtime interpreter — the AST machinery above is compiled in.

Honest Limits

Fish’s friendliness is a deliberate trade, documented rather than hidden. The design document lists POSIX conformance only as its third goal, to be followed “whenever possible without breaking the above goals” (design.rst, L10), and the bash-migration doc opens with the blunter sentence: “fish is intentionally not POSIX-compatible” (fish_for_bash_users.rst, L4). Practically: variables never word-split, there are no heredocs, string manipulation replaces ${foo%bar}, and only * and ** are glob syntax — a non-matching glob fails the command rather than passing a literal * (fish_for_bash_users.rst, L114). Scripts written for sh/bash need porting; fish is not a drop-in /bin/sh replacement. The Rust port is real but young by shell standards — the C++ era left twenty years of optimization history, and the port notes in the changelog are candid that packaging and build dependencies changed wholesale. None of this is instability so much as a stated identity: fish optimizes for the interactive human first, and the source makes that choice visible at every layer.
entry.summary: A source tour of the fish shell's Rust rewrite: the parser, expansion stages, job groups, universal variables, and the reader that make fish feel magic.
